edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De idololatria, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Caeterum quid facient servi vel liberi fideles, item officinales sacrificantibus dominis vel patronis vel praesidibus suis adhaerentes? Sed si merum quis sacrificanti tradiderit, imo si verbo quoque aliquo sacrificio necessario adjuverit, minister habebitur idololatriae. Hujus regulae memores etiam magistratibus et potestatibus officium possumus reddere secundum patriarchas et caeteros majores, qui regibus idololatris usque ad finem idololatriae apparuerunt. Hinc proxime disputatio suborta est, an servus Dei alicujus dignitatis aut potestatis administrationem capiat, si ab omni specie idololatriae intactum se, aut gratia aliqua, aut astutia etiam praestare possit: secundum quod et Joseph, et Daniel mundi ab idololatria exstitere, et dignitatem et potestatem administraverunt in ornamento et purpura totius Aegypti sive Babyloniae. Credamus itaque succedere alicui posse, ut in quoquo honore, ut in solo honoris nomine incedat, neque sacrificet, neque sacrificiis auctoritatem suam accommodet, non hostias locet, non curas templorum deleget, non vectigalia eorum procuret, non spectacula edat de suo aut de publico, aut edendis praesit: nihil solemne pronuntiet vel edicat, ne juret quidem: jam vero quae sunt potestatis, neque judicet de capite alicujus vel pudore (feras enim de pecunia), neque damnet neque praedamnet, neminem vinciat, neminem recludat, aut torqueat; si haec credibile est fieri posse.
pass_a_gloss: But what will the servants or the faithful freemen do, also the artisans adhering to their sacrificing lords or patrons or governors? But if someone has handed over pure wine to the one sacrificing, or even if by some word he has necessarily assisted the sacrifice, he will be considered a minister of idolatry. Being mindful of this rule, we can also render service to magistrates and powers according to the patriarchs and other ancestors, who appeared to idolatrous kings up to the end of idolatry. From this, the dispute has arisen next, whether a servant of God can take on the administration of some dignity or power, if he can keep himself untouched by every kind of idolatry, either by grace or by cunning: according to which also Joseph and Daniel stood out in the world from idolatry and administered dignity and power in the ornament and purple of all Egypt or Babylonia. Let us therefore believe that it is possible for someone to succeed, so that in whatever honor, so that in the sole name of honor he may walk, and not sacrifice, and not accommodate his authority to sacrifices, not place victims, not select the cares of temples, not procure their revenues, not produce spectacles from his own or from public funds, or preside over productions: let him not pronounce or issue anything solemn, nor even swear: now indeed, what are of power, let him not judge concerning the head or shame of anyone (for you will judge concerning money), nor condemn nor sentence, let him not bind anyone, let him not imprison anyone, or torture anyone; if it is believable that these things can be done.

pass_b_english: What about faithful slaves or freedmen, artisans who cling to masters, patrons, or governors who sacrifice? If anyone hands over unmixed wine to a sacrificer, or even assists a sacrifice with a single necessary word, he will be counted a minister of idolatry. Mindful of that rule, we can also render service to magistrates and authorities on the pattern of the patriarchs and other ancestors who served idolatrous kings to the very end of idolatry. This raises the next question: can a servant of God undertake the administration of some dignity or power if he can keep himself untouched by every form of idolatry, whether by grace or even by cunning? Joseph and Daniel, after all, kept themselves clear of idolatry in the world and administered dignity and power wearing the ornament and purple of all Egypt or Babylonia. Let us therefore believe it possible for someone to succeed in such a way that, in whatever honor, he walks in the mere name of honor: he does not sacrifice, does not lend his authority to sacrifices, does not provide victims, does not take charge of temple duties, does not collect their revenues, does not stage spectacles from his own purse or the public treasury, nor preside over them; he issues no solemn pronouncement or decree, not even an oath. As for the functions of power: he does not judge over anyone's head or shame (money cases you will judge), does not condemn or pass sentence, does not bind, imprison, or torture anyone—if that is believable.
